variants.name: Explicit state loop (the transformation the pattern names)
variants.implementation_notes: C has no tail-call guarantee and no annotation for one, so the pattern's realization is the transformation it names: the recursive call becomes a jump back to the top, the parameters become mutable locals (or one state struct), and the base case becomes the loop guard or a break. GCC documents that sibling and tail-recursive calls are optimized when -foptimize-sibling-calls is active (levels -O2, -O3, -Os), so a small self-recursive helper often costs no extra stack in release builds - but the transformation is unspecified: -O0 builds, other compilers, and code with work left after the call all keep the frame. Keep the recursion where it is markedly clearer and depth is bounded by the data; otherwise write the loop.
pitfalls: Release-only elimination: a recursion that is fine under -O2 overflows in a debug or ASan build, or under a compiler that does not run the sibling-call pass, so depth must be bounded independently of the optimization level.

The sibling-call pass can be defeated by mismatched argument sizes, alloca/setjmp in the frame, variadic callees or a different calling convention at an ABI boundary - portability therefore requires the loop.
Nothing diagnoses the loss: C compilers emit no warning when a would-be tail call keeps its frame, so only a depth test or disassembly settles the question.

variants.name: Tail call enforced with Clang musttail
variants.implementation_notes: Clang's musttail attribute makes the tail call a requirement of correctness rather than an optimization: the compiler must generate a tail call even when optimizations are disabled, and it provides assurances that the call is optimized on all targets, not just one. It applies only to a return statement whose value is a function call, and to a callee whose argument and return types are compatible enough for the jump - so the accumulator must be passed in a shape the ABI can forward. Choose it when recursion is the clearest formulation and the toolchain is Clang; GCC offers no counterpart, so the same code needs the loop rewrite there.
pitfalls: The attribute's constraints are strict (matching argument and return types, caller-pop conventions); when they are not met Clang rejects the program instead of silently keeping the frame - that strictness is the point, but it forces helper refactoring.
It is Clang-only: a C library that relies on it stops being portable to GCC/MSVC, which is why the loop rewrite stays the default realization.
